say.text: Three problems before I teach anything. Have a go; the misses are useful.
A well, pink-enough 6-week-old with TOF, no spells and good-sized pulmonary arteries. When is complete repair usually planned?

choices.label: Electively, after the first 3 months of life
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask two things first: is this infant symptomatic, and is there anything high-risk? Then ask which end of the age range a well infant sits at: the first days, or somewhere between.
Right. StatPearls describes deferring complete repair to after the first 3 months of life, and the timing is still debated.

choices.label: Go deeper: other sources on timing

say.text: You picked neonatal repair: tempting, because fixing it earlier sounds safer. What it misses: this infant is well, so there is no push to operate early.
StatPearls describes deferring complete repair to after the first 3 months of life, and the timing is still debated.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so note the qualifier: it is 'a well infant' that gets deferral, not every infant.

say.text: You picked school age: tempting, because waiting sounds safer for a small child. What it misses: the deferral is short, to after the first 3 months, not years.
StatPearls describes deferring complete repair to after the first 3 months of life.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so recheck the unit: months, not school years.

say.text: Not core, so take it with care. One group of authors considers 3-6 months likely ideal for elective repair in asymptomatic patients.
The same authors prefer primary neonatal or early repair for symptomatic infants.
They reserve initial palliation for infants with high-risk features: low birth weight or prematurity, and small or discontinuous pulmonary arteries.
They do not palliate neonates without high-risk features.
Problem two. Some infants need an operation that sends more blood to the lungs before repair.
The Blalock-Taussig shunt connects which two structures?

choices.label: Ascending aorta to right pulmonary artery
Superior vena cava to right pulmonary artery
Subclavian artery to ipsilateral pulmonary artery

say.text: Yes. The Blalock-Taussig shunt connects the subclavian artery to the ipsilateral branch pulmonary artery.
You picked aorta to pulmonary artery: tempting, because the aorta is the obvious systemic source. What it misses: the named origin is the subclavian artery, not the aorta itself.
It connects the subclavian artery to the ipsilateral branch pulmonary artery.
You picked a vein to pulmonary artery: tempting, because veins also drain towards the lungs. What it misses: the Blalock-Taussig shunt is an artery-to-artery connection.
It joins the subclavian artery to the ipsilateral branch pulmonary artery.
Anchor it: subclavian to same-side pulmonary artery.
Want the shunt's role and drawbacks, or move on?

choices.label: Move on to life after repair
Go deeper: palliation and its costs

say.text: Not core, so take it with care. The first surgical treatment of TOF was a palliative subclavian-to-pulmonary-artery shunt by Blalock and Taussig.
Drawbacks include the limited lifespan of the shunt and more late sudden death.
Morbidities of initial palliation include pulmonary artery stenosis and distortion, and smaller pulmonary arteries before repair.
Problem three: the repair is done and years pass. The child needs another operation.
Which is the most common indication for reoperation after TOF repair?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask what the operation itself changed, rather than which old defect might come back. Think about the outflow tract the surgeon had to rebuild.
Yes. Pulmonary insufficiency is the most common indication for reoperation.
You picked residual VSD: tempting, because the old defects seem like the ones that return. What it misses: the repair itself created a new problem.
Pulmonary insufficiency is the most common indication for reoperation.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so reverse the habit: ask what the operation changed.

say.text: You picked recurrent infundibular stenosis: tempting, because the obstruction is the defect you just relieved. What it misses: rebuilding that outflow tract leaves the valve leaking.
Pulmonary insufficiency is the most common indication for reoperation.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so reverse the habit: ask what the operation changed.

say.text: Why does pulmonary regurgitation follow repair? Reason it out.

choices.label: It results from reopening of the VSD patch
It results from reconstruction of the RVOT
It results from left ventricular failure

say.text: Correct. Pulmonary regurgitation results from reconstruction of the RVOT. Pulmonary valve replacement can be done surgically or by a transcatheter approach.
You picked the VSD patch: tempting, because it is the other repair suture line. But the leak is at the pulmonary valve, and the cause is the outflow reconstruction.
Pulmonary regurgitation results from reconstruction of the RVOT.
You picked LV failure: tempting, because heart failure explains many late problems. But this is a right-sided leak, and its cause is the RVOT reconstruction.
Pulmonary regurgitation results from reconstruction of the RVOT.
A 25-year-old had TOF repaired in infancy and asks about the future.
Which statement is true?

choices.label: Repair is curative; arrhythmia risk has ended
Endocarditis risk ended with the repair
Ventricular arrhythmias and sudden death remain risks
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Look at the qualifier in how these risks are described: does the source say 'repaired', 'unrepaired', or both?
Yes. Arrhythmias, including ventricular tachycardia, can occur after repair, and patients with TOF, repaired or unrepaired, are at risk of endocarditis.
You picked cure: tempting, because the anatomy has been fixed. What it misses: the risks outlast the operation.
Arrhythmias, including ventricular tachycardia, can occur after repair. The risk of sudden death is 6-9% 30 years after the procedure.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so recheck: the risks continue after repair.

say.text: You picked endocarditis ending: tempting, because repair sounds like it finishes the problem. What it misses: the source names both groups.
Patients with TOF, repaired or unrepaired, are at risk of endocarditis.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so keep the phrase 'repaired or unrepaired'.

say.text: Up to what share of adults with repaired TOF can have ventricular arrhythmias?
Yes: 40-50% of adults with repaired TOF can have ventricular arrhythmias, and the risk of sudden death is 6-9% 30 years after surgery.
You picked under 1%: tempting, because repair sounds like cure. What it misses: the figure is large.
40-50% of adults with repaired TOF can have ventricular arrhythmias.
Last problem. Without surgery, which is the most frequent cause of death in TOF?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Which would you expect to be most frequent: a vivid late complication, or an event that can happen on any crying bout?
Yes. Hypoxic spells are the most frequent cause of death without surgery, at 68%.
You picked brain abscess: tempting, because it is the vivid complication of chronic hypoxaemia, and it is real. What it misses: it is less frequent.
Brain abscesses account for 13%, and hypoxic spells for 68%.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so let frequency outrank vividness.

say.text: You picked stroke: tempting, because hyperviscosity makes it a known complication. What it misses: it ranks second.
Cerebrovascular accidents account for 17%, and hypoxic spells for 68%.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so let frequency outrank vividness.

Yes: 68% hypoxic spells, 17% cerebrovascular accidents, 13% brain abscesses.

Hypoxic spells 68%, cerebrovascular accidents 17%, brain abscesses 13%.

Which infant is the candidate for initial palliation before repair?

choices.label: A premature infant with small pulmonary arteries
A thriving 4-month-old with good pulmonary arteries

say.text: Right. This source reserves staging with palliation for high-risk features such as prematurity and small pulmonary arteries.
Tempting if you picture TOF as one emergency. But this source does not palliate neonates without high-risk features. The key is the feature, not the age.
Tempting because a shunt sounds safe for any infant. But palliation is reserved for high-risk features, and a thriving infant with good-sized arteries has none; a well infant is repaired electively.
So in the surgical plan for TOF, the Blalock-Taussig shunt is:

choices.label: A palliative shunt, not the definitive repair
The definitive repair of the four defects
A routine first step for every TOF infant
